title: Air India Forms Cost-Cutting Team After Record $2.3 Billion Loss
excerpt: New chief executive Tewolde Gebremariam tightens spending, seeks staff savings ideas and reviews A350 maintenance costs as owners weigh fresh equity.
body:
• Air India has set up a cross-functional cost-cutting team and tightened spending approvals after a loss of more than 220 billion rupees ($2.3 billion) for the year ended March.
  • Chief executive Tewolde Gebremariam, who took charge on August 5, has asked staff for savings ideas under an incentive programme and is reviewing costly A350 engine maintenance contracts.
  • The airline has sought fresh equity from owners Tata Sons and Singapore Airlines, which holds 25.1%; reported figures range from 100 billion rupees to about $1.5 billion.
  • For travellers: no route cuts were announced in this step, but talks to defer aircraft deliveries mean schedules can change — check your booking status before travel and keep airline notifications on.

Air India has created a cross-functional team to find operational savings and tightened spending approval limits after posting a loss of $2.3 billion for the fiscal year ended March, according to Retail News Asia. Chief executive Tewolde Gebremariam told staff in an internal memo that frugality and accountability had to become part of daily decisions, and management will reward employees who submit workable ideas to cut expenses or raise revenue.

A turnaround that has not yet turned

Air India has not recorded an annual profit since returning to private ownership under the Tata Group in 2022. The latest loss, more than 220 billion rupees, was its largest yet. Reporting by Mint, citing Bloomberg, says the airline is also seeking 100 billion rupees in fresh capital from Tata Sons and Singapore Airlines. Retail News Asia put an August equity request at about $1.5 billion. Singapore Airlines holds 25.1% of Air India.

Gebremariam took charge on August 5, succeeding Campbell Wilson. He previously led Ethiopian Airlines, where he built a reputation for lean cost management and commercial expansion. Tata Sons has asked the airline to rein in expansion and consolidate existing operations, Mint reported.

Where the costs are

Fuel prices and longer routings have raised operating costs. Airspace closures over Pakistan and disruption across the Middle East have forced diversions, cancellations and capacity cuts on long-haul services — the routes that matter most to diaspora travellers between India, North America and Europe.

Maintenance is a second front. Air India operates six Airbus A350-900 aircraft with Rolls-Royce Trent XWB engines on India-US and Europe routes, and had ordered 80 such engines with an option for 20 more. Maintenance spending has exceeded the projections in its Airbus Flight Hour Services and Rolls-Royce TotalCare arrangements, and the airline has opened preliminary talks with both providers on lowering those costs, according to the Mint report. Gebremariam has also flagged cargo, which was using only about 35% of capacity.

Fleet renewal adds a third pressure. Shortages of seats and cabin components have delayed retrofits of older aircraft, and management has opened talks to defer deliveries of newly ordered aircraft to conserve capital. Earlier this year, board discussions reported by The Hindu BusinessLine included temporary capacity reductions and lower bonuses — a sign of how long cost pressure has been building.

What it means for passengers

This announcement does not itself cancel routes. The risk for travellers is indirect: deferred deliveries and tighter spending can slow cabin upgrades and make schedules more vulnerable when aircraft are unavailable. Passengers booked on long-haul Air India services in the coming months should monitor their reservations, especially if an aircraft type or timing changes.

What happens next

Two negotiations will determine the pace of the turnaround: the equity terms with Tata Sons and Singapore Airlines, and the maintenance and delivery talks with Airbus, Rolls-Royce and aircraft manufacturers. If fresh capital arrives alongside lower maintenance costs, the airline can protect its long-haul network. If not, the cost team’s work is likely to extend from approval limits to network and capacity decisions.
